title: Before we begin
hookLine: this week remembers a year of deep pain for Sikhs; we go slowly and blame no people as a whole

cards: Some dates, in some families, are said more quietly than others. Ask about 1984 in some Sikh homes, and there may be a long silence before an answer. Or a story about an uncle.
Or a photograph brought out from a drawer. For many Sikh families, 1984 is a wound still within living memory. It isn't a chapter in a book; it's parents, neighbors, a childhood.
So before this week begins, i want to stop for a day and talk about how to walk through it.

teach.b: Here's what this week holds. Tomorrow, Punjab in the early 1980s: how a political crisis became violent. Then June 1984, when the Indian army entered the Harmandir Sahib complex.
Then a library that was lost. Then November 1984, when mobs killed thousands of Sikhs, mostly in Delhi. Then the long wait for justice, and finally how the Sikh community remembers.
Now, how to walk. First: slowly. One piece a day, nothing told for drama.
Second: carefully with the facts. Numbers, causes and people from these years are still argued about. Where accounts differ, i'll say so, and keep to what is widely documented.

teach.h: NO PEOPLE AS A WHOLE TO BLAME.
teach.b: Third, and most important: no people as a whole are to blame. Governments and individuals made choices, and some committed terrible crimes. But no faith and no community is guilty as a whole.
In November, there were Hindu neighbors who hid Sikh families in their homes at great risk. Sikhs themselves hold very different views about the people and choices of those years.
This week asks you to hold more than one thing at once.
Fourth: together. The Sikh word is sangat, the company of others on the path.
Grief carried alone gets heavier; carried in company, it can be held. And fifth: you may stop. If this week is too heavy for you right now, you can wait.
The path will still be here. That, too, honors the memory: coming to it when you can give it your full attention.

how: Sikhs remember 1984 each June and November with Ardas, kirtan and gatherings; many families also speak of it privately, and gently, at home.

games.why: you may continue or wait a while; the path will still be here, and coming with full attention honors the memory.

practice: Take a few slow breaths and notice how you feel about going into this week: curious, heavy, unsure; whatever it is, it's allowed.

Then make a quiet choice, to continue tomorrow or to wait a while and come back; either is fine, and nobody is keeping score. If you do continue, you might decide now who you'd talk to if something weighs on you.
